(p-٥٦١٠) In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

Surah al-Rahman

Al-Mahayimi said: It was named so because it is filled with mention of the magnificent blessings (al-ala'), and the name refers back to this.

It is Meccan, according to the view of Ibn 'Abbas. Its verses number seventy-eight.

Imam Ahmad narrated that the beginning of the mufassal (the later short surahs) according to Ibn Mas'ud was al-Rahman.

(p-٥٦١١) In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[1-2] ﴿The Most Merciful﴾ ﴿taught the Qur'an﴾ [al-Rahman: 2]

﴿The Most Merciful﴾ ﴿taught the Qur'an﴾ [al-Rahman: 2], i.e., He made clear by it what contains His pleasure and what contains His displeasure, out of His mercy, so that He may be obeyed by following what pleases Him, doing what He commanded, and avoiding what He forbade and threatened for, so that abundant reward is attained and one is saved from His painful punishment.

Al-Qadi said: Since the surah is confined to enumerating the worldly and otherworldly blessings, He opened it with "al-Rahman," and He put first what is the root of the religious blessings and the greatest of them, namely His bestowal of the Qur'an and its revelation and teaching, for it is the foundation of the religion, the source of the Sharia, the greatest of revelation, and the most noble of books, since by its inimitability and its inclusion of their essence, it confirms itself and is the confirmation of them.

Then He followed it with His words:

**The commentary on His saying, exalted is He:**

[3–4] ﴿He created man﴾ ﴿taught him expression﴾ [al-Rahman: 4]

﴿He created man﴾ ﴿taught him expression﴾ [al-Rahman: 4]. This is an indication that the creation of humankind, and the expression (al-bayan, "clear expression," meaning the articulation of what is in the heart and the conveying of meaning to others) that distinguishes them from the rest of the animals, is for the sake of what they are able to grasp: receiving revelation, recognizing the truth, and learning the Sacred Law (al-shar', the divine law). That is, if their creation is in reality for this purpose, then it necessitates their connection to the Qur'an, and to its revelation, which is its source and the foundation of its structure.

(p-٥٦١٢) Al-Zamakhshari said: Its being free of a conjunction (al-'atif, the connecting particle such as "wa") is because it comes in the pattern of enumeration, as you say: "Zayd enriched you after poverty, honored you after humiliation, multiplied you after scarcity, and did to you what no one has done to anyone," so how can you deny his kindness? This, as al-Shihab said, is sound. The preferred view is the indication that each of these is perhaps independent and calls for gratitude, and in this there is an indication of their shortcoming in fulfilling it. Had they been joined by a conjunction, despite the strength of their connection and their harmony, it might have been assumed that they were all one single blessing.

Al-Isfahani said in (al-Dhari'a): Since speech is the noblest thing with which humankind is specially endowed, and its intelligible form is that by which it is distinguished from the rest of the animals, the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿He created man﴾ ﴿taught him expression﴾ [al-Rahman: 4], and He did not say "wa 'allamahu" (and taught him). For His saying ﴿taught him﴾ [al-Rahman: 4] has been made an explanation of His saying ﴿He created man﴾, as an alert that His creating him is His specifying him with expression, which, if it were assumed to be removed, humanity would be removed with it. For this reason it was said: "What is man without the tongue but an unattended beast or a formed image?" And it was said: "The person is hidden beneath his tongue."

The poet said:

"The tongue of a young man is half, and half is his heart,
So nothing remains but the form of flesh and blood."

That is: if the speech which is by the tongue is assumed to be removed, and the speaking faculty which is in the heart is assumed to be removed, nothing remains but the form of flesh and blood. So if man is the tongue, there is no doubt that whoever has more of it has more of humanity. Silence, insofar as it is silence, is blameworthy; it is one of the attributes of inanimate objects, let alone animals. God the Exalted has made some animals without voice, and made for some of them voice without articulation. As for one who praises silence, it is by considering those who speak badly, who commit great offenses in matters of religion and worldly affairs through speech. But if they consider themselves, it is absurd to say that silence has merit, let alone that one be given the choice between it and speech. A wise man was asked about the merit of the two, and he said: "Silence is better, until one needs speech." (p-٥٦١٣) Another was asked about their merit, and he said: "Silence from indecency is better than speech in error." From him the poet took:

"Silence is more fitting for a young man
Than speech out of its proper time."

End. It has been permitted, as al-Shihab related, that al-Rahman be the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "Allah is al-Rahman," and what follows is a fresh sentence enumerating His blessings. Then he said: "'Allama" is from ta'lim (teaching), and its object is omitted, i.e., He taught man, not Gabriel or Muhammad, upon them both be blessings and peace. And it is not (from al-'alama, "sign," without estimation), as has been said, i.e., He made him a sign and a proof for whoever reflects; but this is remote.

The discourse on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[5–7] ﴿The sun and the moon [run] by a reckoning﴾ ﴿and the star and the tree prostrate themselves﴾ [al-Rahman: 6] ﴿And the heaven He raised high and set up the balance﴾ [al-Rahman: 7]

﴿The sun and the moon [run] by a reckoning﴾ i.e., they run by a known, determined reckoning in their zodiacal stations (buruj) and their mansions (manazil), by which the affairs of the lower creation are arranged, the seasons and times vary, and the years and reckoning (hisab) are known.

﴿And the star﴾ [al-Rahman: 6] i.e., the plant that "yanjum" (comes forth), that is, that rises out of the earth and has no stem.

﴿And the tree﴾ [al-Rahman: 6] i.e., that which has a stem, ﴿prostrate themselves﴾ [al-Rahman: 6], i.e., they submit to God in what He wills for them by nature, in the manner of the submission of the prostrating one among the accountable, who submits willingly. This is a clear, subordinate metaphor (isti'arah tasrihiyyah tab'iyyah): it likens their course according to the requirement of their nature to the submission of one who prostrates to his Creator. As for the sentence: if it is a predicate (khabar) about the Most Merciful, since it is conjoined to the preceding predicate, then the connecting pronoun is elided for its clarity, i.e., "by His reckoning and they prostrate to Him." Or it is a resumptive sentence (mustaʼnafah), in which case it is cut off because it is directed toward another purpose. The insertion of the conjunction between them is because the sun and the moon are celestial, while the star and the tree are terrestrial, so there is a correspondence (muqabalah) between them, and because all submit to His will.

﴿And the heaven He raised high﴾ [al-Rahman: 7] i.e., He created it raised up.

﴿And set up the balance﴾ [al-Rahman: 7] i.e., justice among His creatures on the earth.

(p-5614) Al-Qashani said: i.e., He lowered the balance of justice to the earth of the soul and the body, for justice (al-'adalah) is a state of the soul, without which human excellence would not be attained. From it comes moderation (al-i'tidal) in the body, which, if it did not exist, would not have come into being nor would it have persisted. And since the affair of religion and of the world is made upright by justice, and the perfection of the soul and body is established through it, such that without it one matter would be corrupted, its observance and preservation were given precedence before enumerating the principles in full, because of the intensity of concern for it and the excessive importance attached to its matter. And His words, exalted is He:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He:

[8–9] ﴿That you not transgress in the balance﴾ ﴿And establish the weight with justice and do not make the balance deficient﴾ [al-Rahman: 9]

﴿That you not transgress in the balance﴾ means: by excess beyond the limit of virtue (al-fadilah, the mean between extremes) and moderation (al-i'tidal, balance), which entails the injustice that causes corruption. The particle "an" (that) is a verbal-source particle (masdariyyah) with the preposition elided, meaning "lest you transgress in it." Or it is an explanatory particle (mufassirah) for what is implied in "He set up the balance," since that carries the sense of speech, because it is through revelation and the informing of the messengers.

﴿And establish the weight with justice﴾ means: uprightness in the way, adherence to the limit of virtue and the point of moderation in all affairs and all faculties.

﴿And do not make the balance deficient﴾ Al-Qashani said: that is, by falling short of the limit of virtue.

Some of the sages said: Justice is the balance of God, Exalted is He. He placed it for creation and set it up for the truth. End of quote.

Among those who interpreted "the balance" in the verse as justice was Mujahid, and Ibn Jarir followed him, as did Ibn Kathir. He supported this with the verse ﴿We certainly sent Our messengers with clear proofs and sent down with them the Scripture and the balance that people may maintain justice﴾ [al-Hadid: 25]. He also permitted that "the balance" be understood as that by which the measures of things are known, such as the scale, the measuring vessel, and the like. From this al-Suyuti said in (al-Iklil): In it is the obligation of justice in weighing and the prohibition of cheating in it. Accordingly, the connection of His words "and He placed the balance" with what precedes it is that, when He described the sky (p-5615) with elevation, which is the source of decrees and measures, He intended to describe the earth and what is in it, through which disparity becomes apparent, by which quantity is known, and by which rights and obligations are equalized. Thus the al-Qadi held, and God knows best.

In reality, the second is one of the instances of the first, and taking the word in its general sense is preferable and more beneficial.

Among the subtleties that the wording of this noble verse allows is the statement of al-Razi:

"The balance is mentioned three times, each time with a different meaning. The first is the instrument; the second is in the sense of the verbal noun (masdar); and the third is in the sense of the object (maf'ul). He said: It is like the Qur'an, which is mentioned with different senses. (One is the sense of connection): His words, Exalted is He: ﴿So follow its recitation﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 18]; and (another is) in the sense of the thing recited, in His words: ﴿Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 17]; and (another is) in the sense of the book containing what is recited, in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And if only a Qur'an by which mountains were moved﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31]. It is then as if it were an instrument and a place for it. And in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿We have given you seven of the oft-repeated and the great Qur'an﴾ [al-Hijr: 87]. Then he said: There is a connection between the Qur'an and the balance, for the Qur'an contains knowledge that is not found in other books, and the balance contains justice that is not found in other instruments." End of quote.

The discussion concerning His saying, Exalted is He:

[10–13] ﴿And the earth He has set down for the creatures.﴾ ﴿Therein is fruit, and palm trees having sheaths.﴾ [Al-Rahman: 11] ﴿And grain having husks, and fragrant plants.﴾ [Al-Rahman: 12] ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?﴾ [Al-Rahman: 13]

﴿And the earth He has set down for the creatures﴾: that is, He spread it out (mahhadaha) for the creation. ﴿Therein is fruit﴾ [Al-Rahman: 11]: that is, kinds of what one enjoys as fruit. ﴿And palm trees having sheaths﴾ [Al-Rahman: 11]: that is, the spathes (awiyat al-tal') of the spadix, which is the thing in which the cluster emerges, then splits open to reveal the clusters, so it becomes unripe dates (busr), then ripe dates (rutab), then it ripens, and its benefit and maturity are complete. They are singled out by mention because of the great benefits in them, as is known from making vessels from them, and benefiting from their heart (jummar), from the spathe, from the unripe dates, from the ripe dates, and other things. Their fruit comes at different times, as if they were different fruits. Thus they are the most complete blessing in comparison with other trees, and for this reason He mentioned the palm tree by its name, and mentioned the fruit without its trees, for the benefits of their trees are in the very fruits themselves.

﴿And grain having husks﴾ [Al-Rahman: 12]: that is, and in it is grain (habb), which is wheat, barley and the like. ﴿Having husks﴾ [Al-Rahman: 12]: that is, dry leaves like chaff. ﴿And fragrant plants﴾ [Al-Rahman: 12]: that is, green leaves, a reminder of the blessing in them and their leaves in their living state. This is according to the reading "al-rayhani" in the genitive (bi-l-jarr). It was also read in the nominative (bi-l-raf'), and it means green crops generally; it was named thus by likening it to what has a spirit (rūḥ), because its vegetative life is in the freshness of its greenness.

Ibn 'Abbas said: al-rayhan is the green of the crops.

Al-Qurtubi said: al-rayhan is either fay'alan from (r-w-ḥ), where the waw became a ya', was assimilated and then lightened; or fi'lan, whose waw was changed to ya' for lightness, or to distinguish it from al-ruhan, which is that which has a spirit (rūḥ).

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?﴾ [Al-Rahman: 13]: Abu al-Su'ud said: the address is to the two species (al-thaqalan), implied by His saying ﴿for the creatures﴾, and His saying ﴿O two species (al-thaqalan)﴾ [Al-Rahman: 31] will follow it. The fa' indicates the sequence of denunciation and reproach for a portion of the varieties of bounties and kinds of favours that necessarily require faith and gratitude. The mention of the title of Lordship, which indicates universal ownership and nurturing, together with its attribution to their pronoun, serves to emphasize the rebuke and intensify the reproach. The Explanation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[14–16] ﴿He created man from clay like pottery﴾ ﴿and He created the jinn from a smokeless flame of fire﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 15] ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 16]

﴿He created man from clay like pottery﴾ Abu al-Su'ud said: This is a preface to the rebuke for their failure to fulfill the obligations of gratitude for the blessing that concerns the essence of each of the two weighty beings (al-thaqalan: humankind and the jinn). Al-salsal (dry clay) is dry earth that makes a ringing sound, and al-fakhkhar is baked earthenware. God Exalted created Adam, peace be upon him, from dust which He made into clay, then into black mud that had been molded, then into dry clay, so there is no contradiction between the verse that speaks of one of these stages and what speaks of another of them.

﴿And He created the jinn﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 15] That is, the jinn, or the father of the jinn, ﴿from smokeless fire﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 15] meaning: from pure flame.

﴿from a flame of fire﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 15] ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 16] meaning: of what He bestowed upon you within the details of your creation of abundant blessings, and of what He made manifest to you through the Qur'an.

The interpretation of His, the Exalted, saying:

[19–21] ﴿He released the two seas, meeting each other.﴾ ﴿Between them is a barrier; they do not transgress.﴾ [al-Rahman: 20] ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ [al-Rahman: 21]

﴿مَرَجَ البَحْرَيْنِ﴾ means He released them, from the phrase "marraja fulanun dabbatahu" (someone let his animal loose), when he left it free and abandoned it. The meaning is: He released and set flowing the salt sea and the sweet sea, ﴿meeting each other﴾, that is, lying side by side.

﴿بَيْنَهُما بَرْزَخٌ﴾ [al-Rahman: 20], that is, a barrier (barzakh) from the power of Allah, the Exalted, and His wondrous creation, ﴿they do not transgress﴾ [al-Rahman: 20], that is, neither of them oversteps against the other by mixing with it and nullifying its distinctive property.

Al-Shihab said: He means that when one of them enters the other, it may flow for parasangs (farasikh) within it without being dissolved and annihilated, until one of them changes the taste and color of the other, as we observe.

It was also said: The intended seas are the Persian Sea and the Roman Sea, for they meet in the Ocean (al-Bahr al-Muhit), and between them is a barrier of land, so they do not pass their boundaries by flooding what lies between them. This is related from Qatadah and al-Hasan. Al-Shihab said: However, it is objected to this view that it does not accord with His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿He released the two seas: this one sweet, palatable, and this one salt, bitter﴾ [al-Furqan: 53], and the Qur'an explains one part of it by another.

Ibn Jarir chose what is related from Ibn 'Abbas and others, that the reference is to the sea of the sky and the sea of the earth, because Allah said: ﴿From them emerge the pearls and the coral﴾, and pearls and coral come only from the shells of the earth's sea, from the drops of rain from the sky. It is known, then, that this refers to the sea of the earth and the sea of the sky. End of quotation.

(p-5619) What applies to the previous view applies to this one as well, namely that it does not accord with that verse, and the basic principle in the verses is that they are mutually consistent.

Ibn Kathir added: What lies between the sky and the earth is not called a barzakh, and "a barrier, forbidden" (hijran mahjuran) [al-Furqan: 22]; so the first view is the preferable one.

﴿فَبِأيِّ آلاءِ رَبِّكُما تُكَذِّبانِ﴾ [al-Rahman: 21], that is, of the benefits in the two seas and in their creation, and He has pointed to some of them in His saying:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 55, verses 22–23:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[22–23] ﴿From them emerge the pearl and the coral.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [al-Rahman: 23]

﴿From them emerge the pearl and the coral.﴾ That is, the large pearls and the small ones. Or (al-marjan) is the well-known red bead. It is said "from them" although it emerges from only one of them, namely the salt water (al-milh), because when the two are mingled, it emerges from them in actuality; or it is that what belongs to one of them is attributed to both of them, just as what proceeds from one member of a group is ascribed to the group. Al-Nasir said: "This is the correct view, and similar to it is His saying: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a man of importance from the two cities?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 31], where only one of the two cities is meant. And it is like saying: 'He is from the people of Egypt,' when he is actually from one quarter of it." End of quote.

Al-Shihab said: It should not be hidden that this – although it is well known – is contrary to the apparent meaning. Either the pronoun in "minhuma" refers to the two seas, Persia and Rome, or it is said that the meaning of its emerging from them is not that it is formed within them, but rather that the two come together in a part of the seas into which the sweet waters flow. End of quote. The matter is easy.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 55, verses 22–23:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[22–23] ﴿From them emerge the pearl and the coral.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [al-Rahman: 23]

﴿From them emerge the pearl and the coral.﴾ That is, the large pearls and the small ones. Or (al-marjan) is the well-known red bead. **Commentary on the interpretation of His saying (Exalted is He):**

[24–25] ﴿And His are the ships, sailing high on the sea like mountains.﴾ ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [al-Rahman: 25]

As for His saying, ﴿And His are the ships﴾, it means the ships, the plural of *jariyah* (ship). ﴿Sailing high on the sea like mountains﴾ has been read with a kasra on the *shin* (*al-munshi'at*), meaning those that are clearly moving along, which come and go. It has also been read with a fatha on the *shin* (*al-munsha'at*), meaning those with raised sails, by which they come and go. *Al-a'lam* is the plural of *'alam*, which is a tall mountain. Since ships are among the greatest means of trade and gain, transporting goods from one land to another and from one region to another, which is beneficial to people in bringing them what they need of all kinds of merchandise, He said: ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [al-Rahman: 25], that is, His blessings which He bestowed through these ships. Al-Qadi said: that is, from His creating their materials, guiding people to take them, and the manner of their construction and their being set afloat on the sea by means that no one other than Him can bring about the creation and assembly of.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 55, verses 26–28:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[26–28] ﴿Everyone upon it is passing away.﴾ ﴿And there remains the Face of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honor.﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 27] ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 28]

﴿Everyone upon it is passing away﴾ means: whoever is upon the surface of the earth is perishing.

﴿And there remains the Face of your Lord﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 27] means: His noble Essence. ﴿Owner of Majesty﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 27] means: of greatness, exaltedness and magnificence. ﴿And Honor﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 27] means: of general bounty. This verse is like His saying: ﴿Everything will perish except His Face﴾ [Al-Qasas: 88].

Since the passing away of creation is the means of their resurrection to the second creation (al-nash'ah al-ukhra), by which the righteous is distinguished from the falsifier, the first is turned to reward, and the other returns with punishment, and this is among the greatest blessings in which the Divine justice encompasses those who are accountable, He, glorified is He, said: ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 28]

Al-Razi has indicated the benefits contained in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Everyone upon it is passing away﴾, saying: In it are benefits:

Among them: urging worship, and spending the brief time on obedience.

Among them: preventing reliance on what one possesses, so that when a person is in blessing he does not say, "It will never leave," thereby abandoning return to God, relying on his wealth and property.

Among them: commanding patience if one is in harm, so that he does not disbelieve in God on the basis that the matter will go away and the harm will cease.

Among them: abandoning the taking of others as objects of worship, and restraining from being deceived by closeness to what is owned, and abandoning seeking nearness to God, Exalted; for their affair is near to cessation.

Among them: the excellence of monotheism, and abandoning both apparent and hidden polytheism altogether, because the one who passes away is not fit to be worshipped.

The discussion of the words of His saying, Exalted is He:

[29–30] ﴿Whatever is in the heavens and the earth asks of Him. Every day He is in a matter.﴾ ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [al-Rahman: 29–30]

﴿Whatever is in the heavens and the earth asks of Him﴾ means: they call upon Him, turn to Him in longing, and hope for His mercy, because of their essential poverty and His absolute self-sufficiency.

﴿Every day He is in a matter﴾ means: at every moment He brings about affairs and renews conditions. Mujahid said: He gives to the one who asks, releases the captive, answers the one who calls, and heals the sick.

Ibn Jarir narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited this verse, and it was said: "O Messenger of Allah! And what is that matter?" He said: "He forgives a sin, relieves a distress, raises some peoples and lowers others."

Al-Qashani said: The intended meaning is that everything asks Him, so the rational beings are overshadowed, and the expression "man" (من) is used, meaning: everything asks Him, through the tongue of readiness (isti'dad) and need, constantly. ﴿Every day He is in a matter﴾ by pouring out what each thing deserves and merits according to its readiness. Whoever prepares himself by purification and cleansing for the perfections of goodness and the lights, He pours them upon him together with the existence of that readiness; and whoever prepares himself by clouding the essence of his soul with dark states and vices, and defiles his beliefs with corrupt doctrines and wickedness, toward evils, hateful things, and kinds of pains, calamities, punishment and ruin, He pours those upon him together with the existence of that readiness. End of quotation.

Those who took the verse in its general sense with regard to the askers, and specifically with regard to the tongue of readiness and other than it, such as Ibn Kathir and al-Qadi, saw it as specific to rational beings, and general in the tongue of state or speech. The closer view is what comes first to understanding, and that is what we mentioned first. ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [al-Rahman: 30] meaning: of what fulfills your request and brings forth for you, from the hidden store of His power and creation, moment by moment.

The discussion of the words of His Exalted saying:

[31–32] ﴿We will attend to you, O you two burdens﴾ ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [al-Rahman: 32]

﴿We will attend to you, O you two burdens﴾. Al-Qurtubi said: It is said, "I became free from the occupation (faraghtu min al-shughl), I become free (afrigh) with freedom (faraghan) and emptying (furuqan)," and "I devoted myself (tafarraghtu) to such-and-such," and "I exhausted my effort (istafrightu majhudi) in such-and-such," meaning: I expended it. God Exalted has no occupation from which He becomes free; rather the meaning is: We will set Our intention to requite you or to call you to account. It is therefore a warning and a threat to them, like the saying of one who wishes to threaten someone: "Then I will attend to you," meaning: I will target you.

Al-Zajjaj said: Emptiness (al-faragh) in the language is of two kinds: one of them is freedom from occupation, and the other is intending a thing and turning toward it, as here, and it is a threat and warning. You say: "I have become free of what I was engaged in," meaning: my preoccupation with it has ceased. And you say: "I will attend to so-and-so," meaning: I will make him my intention. So it is by way of figurative representation: He, Exalted, likened His management of the matter of the Hereafter, by taking up the requital and delivering reward and punishment to the accountable, after His management of the affairs of this world by command and prohibition, by causing death and life, by withholding and giving, and that no matter preoccupies Him, to the case of one who, when he is occupied with one task that keeps him from another, once he is free of that task, begins another. The clear metaphor (al-isti'arah al-tasrihiyyah) is also permissible. The author of al-Miftah (ṣāḥib al-Miftāḥ) touched on this when he said: "Al-faragh is deliverance from pressing affairs; and God, Mighty and Majestic, is not preoccupied by one matter from another; it has been used metaphorically for taking up the requital alone."

A subtle point:

The word ayyuhā is written without an alif. As for pronunciation, Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read ayyuhā with an alif in pause; the rest pause on the written form ayyuhā with a sukun on the ha'. In continuation, Ibn 'Amir read ayyuhu with a damma on the ha', and the rest with a fatha on it.

And ﴿al-thaqalān﴾ is the dual of (thaqal), with two fathas, a form fa'al in the sense of maf'al, because they burdened the earth, or in the sense of maf'ul, because they were burdened with obligations. Al-Hasan said: because of their weight with sins.

The address in "lakum" has been said to be to the criminals, but His saying "ayyuhā al-thaqalān" rejects that. Yes! The intended object of the threat is them, and there is no barrier to threatening all by His saying, as al-Shihab stated. And from this noble expression is not understood a pure threat; rather it also carries a promise, because the meaning is: We will attend to your reckoning, so We will reward the people of obedience and punish the disobedient, and this is evident. Therefore He counted that as a favor upon them in His saying: ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [al-Rahman: 32], that is, of His reward to the people of obedience and His punishment to the people of disobedience.

**The Explanation of His Words, Exalted is He:**

﴿O assembly of jinn and mankind, if you are able to pass beyond the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass through. You will not pass through except with authority﴾ ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?﴾ [al-Rahman: 34]

﴿O assembly of jinn and mankind, if you are able to pass beyond the regions of the heavens and the earth﴾: i.e., to cross the extremities of the heavens and the earth, thereby escaping your Lord, i.e., by leaving His dominion, the seat of His authority and His kingdom, so that He cannot overpower you. ﴿Then pass through﴾: i.e., cross over and go out. ﴿You will not pass through except with authority﴾: i.e., with strength, dominion and overpowering might. And how could you possess that? Compare His words: ﴿And you cannot escape Him on earth or in heaven﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 22].

It has also been said that the meaning of the verse is: if you are able to know what is in the heavens and the earth, then know it; but you will not know it except with authority, meaning clear proof from God Most High. The first interpretation is more apparent, because when He mentioned in the previous verse that there is inevitably a Recompense for the servants, He followed it with His words: ﴿if you are able﴾, etc., to show that they have no power to escape His requital and punishment if He wills it.

﴿So which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?﴾ [al-Rahman: 34] Ibn Jarir said: i.e., [the favor] of the equality among all of you, in that none of you is able to oppose a command that He has willed for you.

The judge (al-Qadi) said: i.e., [the favor] of admonition, warning, leniency and pardon, together with His complete power.

The interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[35–36] ﴿A flame of fire and molten brass will be sent against you both, and you will have no defense.﴾ ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord will you both deny?﴾ [al-Rahman: 35–36]

﴿A flame of fire will be sent against you both﴾, meaning: a blaze of fire. ﴿And molten brass﴾, meaning: yellow brass that is melted and poured (p-5625) over their heads. ﴿And you will have no defense﴾, meaning: you will be unable to resist and will not be rescued from it. The meaning is that if you persist in disbelief, defiance, and disobedience toward the Messenger, then in the Hereafter nothing awaits you but this painful punishment.

Ibn Kathir went to the view that this verse and what precedes it are addressed to the disbelievers in the Hereafter. His words are: "This is in the station of the gathering, when the angels surround the creatures, so no one can go anywhere ﴿except with authority﴾ [al-Rahman: 33], meaning by the command of Allah. ﴿On that Day, man will say: Where is the escape?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 10] ﴿No! There is no refuge!﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 11] ﴿To your Lord, on that Day, is the place of rest﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 12]." And He, Exalted is He, said:

﴿As for those who earned evil deeds, the recompense of an evil deed is its equivalent, and humiliation will cover them. They will have no protector from Allah. It is as if their faces were covered with pieces of the dark night. They are the companions of the Fire; therein they will abide forever﴾ [Yunus: 27]. Therefore He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿A flame of fire will be sent against you both, and molten brass, and you will have no defense.﴾ The meaning is: if you were to flee on the Day of Resurrection, the angels and the Zabaniyah (the angels of punishment) would drive you back by sending down blazing fire and melted brass upon you, so that you return." End of quotation.

Then I saw that Imam Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, had preceded him to this. At the end of his book (Tariq al-Hijratayn), in explaining this verse, after mentioning something like the two interpretations we have already presented concerning His saying ﴿If you are able to pass through﴾ [al-Rahman: 33], he said the following:

"There is another explanation of the verse: this address is in the Hereafter, when the angels surround the regions of the earth and the enclosure (surādiq) of the Fire encompasses the horizons. Then the creatures flee, but they find no escape and no passage, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿O my people, I fear for you the Day of Calling Out﴾ [Ghafir: 32] ﴿The Day you will turn back, fleeing﴾ [Ghafir: 33]. Mujahid said: fleeing, unable to escape. Al-Dahhak said: when they hear the roaring of the Fire, they scatter in flight, but they do not reach any region without finding the angels in ranks, so they return to the place where they were. That is His saying: ﴿And the angel will be upon its edges﴾ [al-Haqqah: 17], and His saying: ﴿O assembly of jinn and mankind﴾ [al-Rahman: 33], and so on. This view is more evident, and Allah knows best. When the creatures appear, they turn their backs in flight, and it is said to them: ﴿If you are able to pass through the regions of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Rahman: 33], meaning: if you are able to go beyond the regions of the heavens and the earth and thus overcome your Lord so that He cannot punish you, then do it.

Before it is ﴿We will attend to you, O two burdened ones﴾ [al-Rahman: 31], and this is in the Hereafter; after it is ﴿When the sky is split open﴾ [al-Rahman: 37], and this too is in the Hereafter. ﴿A flame of fire will be sent against you both﴾, meaning: a blaze of fire. ﴿And molten brass﴾, meaning: yellow brass that is melted and poured (p-5625) over their heads. ﴿And you will have no defense﴾, meaning: you will be unable to resist and will not be rescued from it. The meaning is that if you persist in disbelief, defiance, and disobedience toward the Messenger, then in the Hereafter nothing awaits you but this painful punishment.

Ibn Kathir went to the view that this verse and what precedes it are addressed to the disbelievers in the Hereafter. There is no refuge!﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 11] ﴿To your Lord, on that Day, is the place of rest﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 12]." And He, Exalted is He, said:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 55, verses 37–38:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[37–38] ﴿And when the sky splits open and becomes red like rose and like oil(dregs)﴾ ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [al-Rahman: 38]

ALQASIMI'S COMMENTARY (MAHASIN AL-TA'WIL) ON SURAH 55, VERSES 39–40

On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[39–40] ﴿So on that Day, no inquiry will be made of any human or jinn about his sin.﴾ ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [al-Rahman: 40]

﴿So on that Day, no inquiry will be made of any human or jinn about his sin.﴾ That is: no door of excuse will be opened for him, like His saying: ﴿And it will not be permitted for them to make excuses﴾ [al-Mursalat: 36]. Thus, in the "inquiry" there is a metaphor for the negation of hearing an excuse; it is of the type of negating the cause in order to negate the effect. Many scholars, however, took the "inquiry" literally and tried to reconcile it with what may seem to contradict it.

Al-Qashani said: As for the "standing" and the "inquiry" referred to in His saying, ﴿Stop them, for they are to be questioned﴾ [al-Saffat: 24], and its like, they belong to another station within that long Day, whose duration is fifty thousand years. This station may come before the first station of that Day, and it may come after it.

Ibn Kathir likewise said: This verse is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿This is a Day when they will not speak﴾ [al-Mursalat: 35] ﴿And it will not be permitted for them to make excuses﴾ [al-Mursalat: 36]. That is one state, and there is another state in which He questions all creatures about all their deeds. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely question them all, about what they used to do﴾ [al-Hijr: 92–93]. And there is another interpretation of the verse. Mujahid said: The angels will not ask about the criminal; they will recognize them by their marks.

Imam Ibn al-Qayyim said in (Tariq al-Hijratayn): It has been differed over regarding this negated inquiry. It was said: it is the time of resurrection and the going forth to the place of standing; at that time they will not be questioned, and they will be questioned after prolonged standing and their seeking intercession with God that He judge them and relieve them from that station. It was also said: what is negated is the inquiry of seeking information and asking for knowledge, not the inquiry of reckoning and recompense; that is, God already knows their sins, so He does not question them about them as one who wishes to know them, but He calls them to account for them. End of quote.

﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [al-Rahman: 40] Ibn Jarir said: That is, from His justice toward you is that He does not punish any of you except a criminal.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying:

[41–45] ﴿The criminals will be known by their marks, so they will be seized by the forelocks and the feet.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ [al-Rahman: 42] ﴿This is Hell, which the criminals denied.﴾ [al-Rahman: 43] ﴿They will go around between it and scalding hot water.﴾ [al-Rahman: 44] ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ [al-Rahman: 45]

﴿The criminals will be known by their marks﴾ means: by the gloom, grief and humiliation that will cover them. It was also said: by the blackness of their faces and the blueness of their eyes. ﴿So they will be seized by the forelocks and the feet﴾ means: the angels of punishment (al-Zabaniyah) will seize them by their forelocks and their feet, drag them towards Hell, and hurl them into it. The *ba'* (bi) here is for instrumentality, as in "I took hold of the halter (bi al-khitam)," or it is for transitivity. The *nasiyah* (forelock) is the front part of the head.

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ [al-Rahman: 42] Ibn Jarir said: that is, from His making His angels know the criminals among you, from among the people of obedience, so that the criminals alone are singled out for humiliation and disgrace, apart from others.

﴿This is Hell, which the criminals denied.﴾ [al-Rahman: 43] ﴿They will go around between it and scalding hot water.﴾ [al-Rahman: 44] *Hamim* means hot water, and *ani* means that its heat has reached its limit and its boiling has become intense. Everything that has ripened and reached its completion is said to have *ana*, and from this is His saying: ﴿not waiting for its ripeness (inahu)﴾ [al-Ahzab: 53], meaning its maturity and its reaching completion. ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ [al-Rahman: 45] That is: from His punishment of those who disbelieve in Him, and His honouring of those who believe in Him.

The commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on Surah 55, verses 46–59:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[46–59] ﴿And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾ ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 47] ﴿Having many branches﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 48] ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 49] ﴿In them are two flowing springs﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 50] ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 51] ﴿In them are two of every fruit, a pair﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 52] (p-5630) ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 53] ﴿Reclining on beds whose linings are of brocade, and the fruit of the two gardens will be within reach﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 54] ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 55] ﴿In them are those restraining their gaze, whom no man or jinn has touched before them﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 56] ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 57] ﴿As if they were rubies and coral﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 58] ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 59]

[46–59] ﴿And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾ ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 47] ﴿Having many branches﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 48] ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 49] ﴿In them are two flowing springs﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 50] ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 51] ﴿In them are two of every fruit, a pair﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 52] (p-5630) ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 53] ﴿Reclining on beds whose linings are of brocade, and the fruit of the two gardens will be within reach﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 54] ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 55] ﴿In them are those restraining their gaze, whom no man or jinn has touched before them﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 56] ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 57] ﴿As if they were rubies and coral﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 58] ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 59]

﴿And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord﴾: that is, his standing before his Lord for the reckoning, so that he obeys Him by performing His obligations and avoiding His prohibitions. Its attribution to the Lord is because it is in His presence, like the saying of the Arabs: "a she-camel that lies down at milking" (raqud al-halb), meaning one that lies down at the time of milking. Or it is the place where the servants stand for the reckoning, and its attribution to the Lord is a lam of exclusivity (lam al-milkiyya), because sovereignty on that day belongs exclusively to Him, may He be exalted. Or it is a kinaya (an indirect, allusive expression) for the fear of the Lord, and an affirmation of His fear for the servant by way of an eloquent demonstrative argument, because whoever feels fear in the presence of someone reveres him even when that person is not there; so his fear of Him is by way of greater priority. This is like what the eloquent writers say: "the lofty station" and "the exalted assembly." ﴿Two gardens﴾: that is, a garden for whoever among mankind obeys, and a garden for whoever among the jinn obeys. Or it is a kinaya for the multiplication of the reward, and the choice of the dual form is for the rhyme (fasila). ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 47]: that is, by His rewarding the doer of good with what has been described.

﴿Having many branches﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 48]: that is, kinds of trees and fruits. It is the plural of (fann), meaning "kind," or it means soft branches, the plural of (fanan), which is what is thin and supple from the branch.

﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 49] ﴿In them are two flowing springs﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 50] ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 51] ﴿In them are two of every fruit, a pair﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 52] ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 53] ﴿Reclining on beds whose linings are of brocade﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 54]: brocade (istabraq) is what is thick of silk (dibaj). He draws attention to the nobility of the outer surface by the nobility of the lining, and this is of the type of alerting to the higher by means of the lower.

Ibn Mas'ud said: "These are the linings; so how would it be if you saw the outer surfaces?!"

﴿And the fruit of the two gardens will be within reach﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 54]: that is, their fruit that is gathered is near at hand in its clusters. ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 55] ﴿In them are those restraining their gaze﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 56]: that is, lowering their eyelids, lowering their glances, not looking eagerly at what is far away, and not looking at anyone other than their husbands. Or its meaning is: the sight does not go beyond them, like the saying of al-Mutanabbi:

"And a slender waist on which eyes rest, as if around it is a girdle of pupils."

So the meaning is: they restrain the gaze of others from going beyond them to other women. Or the meaning is: intensely white in the whites of their eyes, as one says: "one with beautiful large eyes" (ahwar al-tarf) and "one who is beautiful-eyed" (hawra'), from the expression "a garment that is carefully made" (thawb maqsur) and "fine white cloth" (hawwari).

It is clear that these meanings here do not conflict, since all of them are realized in their reality. ﴿Whom no man or jinn has touched before them﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 56]: that is, has not touched them. Its origin is the emergence of blood, and for this reason menstruation is called (tamth). Then it was applied to intercourse with virgins, because of the blood that emerges from it, and then it became general for any intercourse. It may be said that the expression with it is an indication that they are found virgin every time they are had intercourse with. The verse is used as evidence that the jinn also have intercourse and enter Paradise.

﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 57] ﴿As if they were rubies and coral﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 58]: that is, in beauty and radiance, or in the redness of the cheek and face, out of modesty and shyness. ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 59]

**[The interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:]**

[60–78] ﴿Is the reward of good anything but good?﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ [55:61] ﴿And besides them are two gardens,﴾ [55:62] ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ [55:63] ﴿Dark green.﴾ [55:64] [p-5632] ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ [55:65] ﴿In them are two fountains gushing forth.﴾ [55:66] ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ [55:67] ﴿In them are fruits, palm trees and pomegranates.﴾ [55:68] ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ [55:69] ﴿In them are good and beautiful [women].﴾ [55:70] ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ [55:71] ﴿Maidens, secluded in pavilions.﴾ [55:72] ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ [55:73] ﴿Untouched before them by man or jinn.﴾ [55:74] ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ [55:75] ﴿Reclining on green cushions and beautiful rugs.﴾ [55:76] ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ [55:77] ﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honour.﴾ [55:78]

﴿Is the reward of good anything but good?﴾ That is, for the deed. ﴿Anything but good﴾ means, in the reward, which is Paradise. ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ [55:61] ﴿And besides them﴾ [55:62], that is, besides those two mentioned gardens, ﴿are two gardens﴾ [55:62], that is, two other orchards, indicating the abundance of the gardens, their continuity, and the wide extent of the gaze over their scenes.

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ [55:63] ﴿Dark green﴾ [55:64]: that is, verdant from being well watered, [p-5633] inclining towards blackness because of the intensity of the greenness. Or, from the abundance of their trees, extending without end.

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ [55:65] ﴿In them are two fountains gushing forth﴾ [55:66]: that is, two springs bubbling forth with water.

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ [55:67] ﴿In them are fruits, palm trees and pomegranates﴾ [55:68]. He singled them out for mention to make clear their excellence, as if, because of the distinction they have, they were two other kinds.

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ [55:69] ﴿In them are good [women]﴾ [55:70]: this is the plural of khayyirah (good, excellent), with the doubling removed, though it has been read according to the original form, that is, those of excellent character. The choice of the feminine pronoun rather than the dual is out of regard for the word that follows it as its predicate: ﴿beautiful﴾ [55:70], that is, beautiful of face.

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ [55:71] ﴿Maidens, secluded in pavilions﴾ [55:72]. Hur (maidens) is the plural of hawra' (a woman with pure white eyes), meaning the white and pure. The meaning of ﴿secluded﴾ [55:72] is that they have confined themselves to their dwellings, and their only concern is their adornment and their pastimes. The meanings mentioned earlier also apply to it. And ﴿pavilions﴾ [55:72]: Ibn Jarir said: by it is meant houses. The Arabs sometimes call women's litters "pavilions" and he then recited a verse as evidence for this.

﴿In them are women restraining their gaze, whom no man or jinn has touched before them﴾ [55:56]. By these he means the maidens of the two gardens which are besides the first two. Or it is a repetition of what preceded, to draw attention to this attribute, and to its being at the forefront of desirable things and the vanguard of delights:

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ [55:75] ﴿Reclining on cushions﴾ [55:76], that is, couches, or supports, or pillows, ﴿green﴾ [55:76] ﴿and beautiful rugs﴾ [55:76], that is, carpets and mats, ﴿beautiful﴾ [55:76], that is, excellent. **Benefit:**

Regarding what the scholars said about the secret of the repetition of "So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?", al-Suyuti said in al-Itqan, in the section on repetition:

Repetition may sometimes not be for emphasis in terms of technical craft, though it is meaningfully emphatic. Among it is that in which a separation occurs between the two repeated items, for emphasis is not separated from what it emphasises.

Then he said: Among this is the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: "So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?" For although it is repeated over thirty-some times, each instance relates to what precedes it, and for this reason it exceeded three. Had all of them referred to one thing, it would not have exceeded three, because emphasis does not exceed that. This was said by Ibn Abd al-Salam and others. The end.

In Arus al-Afrah: If you say: when what is meant by each is what precedes it, is that not elaboration? Rather, they are expressions, each of which is meant to be something other than what the other is meant to be?

I say: If we say that what counts is the generality of the expression, then each one is meant to be what the other is meant to be, but it is repeated so that it is explicit in what follows it and apparent in other respects.

If you say: does that entail emphasis?

I say: The matter is so, and it is not objected that emphasis is not increased beyond three, because that applies to emphasis which is a follower. As for mentioning a thing in more than three separate contexts, there is nothing preventing it. The end.

Al-Izz ibn Abd al-Salam said at the end of his book al-Isharah ila al-Ijaz: As for His saying, "So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?", it may be repeated over all His bounties; it may be that each instance refers to the bounty between it and the one before it; it may be that the first refers to the bounties preceding it, the second to those preceding it, the third to those preceding the first, and the fourth to those preceding the first, second and third, and so on to the end of the surah. [p-5636]

If it is said: how can His saying, "We will attend to you, O two worlds [of men and jinn]" [55:31], be a bounty, and His saying, "The guilty will be known by their marks" [55:41], be a bounty? Likewise, His saying, "This is Hell, which the guilty deny" [55:43], and His saying, "There will be sent against you both a flame of fire and molten brass" [55:35], and His saying, "They will go around between it and scalding water, intensely hot" [55:44]?

We say: all of these are great bounties, because Allah threatens His servants with them for their reform, so that they leave the realm of disbelief, rebellion, wickedness and disobedience for the realm of obedience, faith, submission and compliance. For whoever warns against the path of destruction, and explains the harm it contains, and urges the path of safety that leads to reward and honour, is a benefactor in the utmost degree and a doer of the utmost good. Similar to this is His saying, "This is what the Most Merciful promised" [36:52]. On this basis, there is suitability for the connection through mention of the attribute of mercy in that context. As for His saying, "Everyone upon it will perish" [55:26], it is a reminder of death and annihilation, to encourage turning towards deeds for the abode of permanence, and turning away from the abode of perishing. The end.

Al-Baghawi said: This verse is repeated in thirty-one places to affirm the bounty and to emphasise the reminder of it. Then He enumerated His blessings to creation, separating each two bounties with what alerts them to it, so that He makes them understand the bounties and confirms them concerning them, like the saying of a man to one who has done him good and bestowed upon him favours while denying and disbelieving them: "Were you not poor and I made you rich? Will you deny this? Were you not naked and I clothed you? Will you deny this? Were you not obscure and I made you honoured? Will you deny this?" Such speech is common in Arabic discourse. The end.

[p-5637] Al-Sayyid Murtada said in al-Durar wal-Ghurar: The repetition in Surat al-Rahman is only made beautiful for the sake of affirming the varied and enumerated bounties. So whenever He mentions a bounty He has bestowed, He rebukes for denial, as a man says to another: "Did I not treat you well by making you wealthy in property? Did I not treat you well by doing such-and-such for you?" So repetition is fitting here, because what is affirmed by it differs, and this is common in Arabic speech and poetry, like the saying of Muhalhil lamenting Kulayb:

"Is it not justice from Kulayb / when the neighbours of the protector are wronged?"

"Is it not justice from Kulayb / when the acacias tremble from the north wind?"

"Is it not justice from Kulayb / when the veiled women come out?"

"Is it not justice from Kulayb / when the secrets of affairs are made public?"

"Is it not justice from Kulayb / when what is feared of the frontiers is feared?"

"Is it not justice from Kulayb / on the day of the great affair's turmoil?"

"Is it not justice from Kulayb / when the protector of the seeker of refuge gives way?"

Then he recited other odes in this pattern, which is one of the subtleties of the Arabs. Understand it.

Shaykh al-Islam said in Mutashabih al-Qur'an: This verse is mentioned thirty-one times. Eight of them are mentioned after verses listing the wonders of Allah's creation and the marvels of His making, and the origin of creation and their return. Then seven of them come after verses mentioning Hell and its severities, corresponding to the number of the gates of Hell. Mentioning the bounties after them is fitting, because among the bounties is the removal of affliction and the postponement of punishment. After these seven, there are eight describing the two gardens and their people, corresponding to the number of the gates of Paradise, and eight more after them, describing the two gardens which are besides the two gardens, taken from His saying, "And besides them are two gardens" [55:62]. Whoever believes in the first eight and acts in accordance with them deserves those two groups of eight from Allah, and is protected from the previous seven. The end.

O Allah, increase us in awareness of the subtleties of Your Noble Qur'an, and in plunging into the pearls of Your Great Criterion.

We say: all of these are great bounties, because Allah threatens His servants with them for their reform, so that they leave the realm of disbelief, rebellion, wickedness and disobedience for the realm of obedience, faith, submission and compliance. "Is it not justice from Kulayb / when the veiled women come out?"

"Is it not justice from Kulayb / when the secrets of affairs are made public?"

"Is it not justice from Kulayb / when what is feared of the frontiers is feared?"

"Is it not justice from Kulayb / on the day of the great affair's turmoil?"

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ [55:63] ﴿Dark green﴾ [55:64]: that is, verdant from being well watered, [p-5633] inclining towards blackness because of the intensity of the greenness. Or, from the abundance of their trees, extending without end.

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ [55:65] ﴿In them are two fountains gushing forth﴾ [55:66]: that is, two springs bubbling forth with water.

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ [55:67] ﴿In them are fruits, palm trees and pomegranates﴾ [55:68]. He singled them out for mention to make clear their excellence, as if, because of the distinction they have, they were two other kinds.

The Arabs sometimes call women's litters "pavilions" and he then recited a verse as evidence for this.

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ [55:63] ﴿Dark green﴾ [55:64]: that is, verdant from being well watered, [p-5633] inclining towards blackness because of the intensity of the greenness. Or, from the abundance of their trees, extending without end.

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ [55:65] ﴿In them are two fountains gushing forth﴾ [55:66]: that is, two springs bubbling forth with water.

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ [55:67] ﴿In them are fruits, palm trees and pomegranates﴾ [55:68]. He singled them out for mention to make clear their excellence, as if, because of the distinction they have, they were two other kinds.

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ [55:69] ﴿In them are good [women]﴾ [55:70]: this is the plural of khayyirah (good, excellent), with the doubling removed, though it has been read according to the original form, that is, those of excellent character. The choice of the feminine pronoun rather than the dual is out of regard for the word that follows it as its predicate: ﴿beautiful﴾ [55:70], that is, beautiful of face.

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ [55:71] ﴿Maidens, secluded in pavilions﴾ [55:72]. Hur (maidens) is the plural of hawra' (a woman with pure white eyes), meaning the white and pure. The meaning of ﴿secluded﴾ [55:72] is that they have confined themselves to their dwellings, and their only concern is their adornment and their pastimes. The meanings mentioned earlier also apply to it. And ﴿pavilions﴾ [55:72]: Ibn Jarir said: by it is meant houses. The Arabs sometimes call women's litters "pavilions" and he then recited a verse as evidence for this.

﴿In them are women restraining their gaze, whom no man or jinn has touched before them﴾ [55:56]. By these he means the maidens of the two gardens which are besides the first two. Or it is a repetition of what preceded, to draw attention to this attribute, and to its being at the forefront of desirable things and the vanguard of delights:

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ [55:75] ﴿Reclining on cushions﴾ [55:76], that is, couches, or supports, or pillows, ﴿green﴾ [55:76] ﴿and beautiful rugs﴾ [55:76], that is, carpets and mats, ﴿beautiful﴾ [55:76], that is, excellent. The adjective is clarifying, and for this reason Ibn Jubayr said: "The 'abqari' are the finest rugs," that is, their excellent ones.

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ [55:77]: that is, of His honouring the people of His obedience with this honour from you two. ﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honour﴾ [55:78], that is, Possessor of greatness and majesty, of bestowing favours. Here "name" is a metonymy for the Exalted Essence, because the verb mentioned has frequently been joined with it, as in the verse ﴿Blessed is He who placed in the sky constellations﴾ [25:61] and the verse ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is dominion﴾ [67:1], and similar verses. It has also been said that the word "name" is superfluous, like the verse:

"Until the year's end, then 'peace be upon you both'"

As for the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, "Blessed is the name of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honour," it is true. The meaning of "tabaraka" is "taf'ala" from "barakah" (blessing). Blessing is due to the name of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, which is a word composed of letters of the alphabet. We seek blessing by mentioning Him, by glorifying Him, by revering and honouring Him. So to Him belongs blessing, and to Him belongs reverence from us and from Allah, Exalted is He, and to Him belongs honour from Allah, Exalted is He, and from us, whether it is written on paper, or on something inscribed in it, or mentioned by tongues. Whoever does not revere the name of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, [p-5635] in this way, nor honours it, is an unbeliever without doubt. So the verse is to be taken in its apparent sense without interpretation, and their clinging to it is thereby void. The end of his words, may Allah have mercy on him.

**Benefit:**

Regarding what the scholars said about the secret of the repetition of "So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?", al-Suyuti said in al-Itqan, in the section on repetition:

Repetition may sometimes not be for emphasis in terms of technical craft, though it is meaningfully emphatic. Among it is that in which a separation occurs between the two repeated items, for emphasis is not separated from what it emphasises.

Then he said: Among this is the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: "So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?" For although it is repeated over thirty-some times, each instance relates to what precedes it, and for this reason it exceeded three. Had all of them referred to one thing, it would not have exceeded three, because emphasis does not exceed that. This was said by Ibn Abd al-Salam and others. The end.

In Arus al-Afrah: If you say: when what is meant by each is what precedes it, is that not elaboration? Rather, they are expressions, each of which is meant to be something other than what the other is meant to be?

I say: If we say that what counts is the generality of the expression, then each one is meant to be what the other is meant to be, but it is repeated so that it is explicit in what follows it and apparent in other respects.

If you say: does that entail emphasis?

I say: The matter is so, and it is not objected that emphasis is not increased beyond three, because that applies to emphasis which is a follower. As for mentioning a thing in more than three separate contexts, there is nothing preventing it. The end.

Al-Izz ibn Abd al-Salam said at the end of his book al-Isharah ila al-Ijaz: As for His saying, "So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?", it may be repeated over all His bounties; it may be that each instance refers to the bounty between it and the one before it; it may be that the first refers to the bounties preceding it, the second to those preceding it, the third to those preceding the first, and the fourth to those preceding the first, second and third, and so on to the end of the surah. [p-5636]

If it is said: how can His saying, "We will attend to you, O two worlds [of men and jinn]" [55:31], be a bounty, and His saying, "The guilty will be known by their marks" [55:41], be a bounty? Likewise, His saying, "This is Hell, which the guilty deny" [55:43], and His saying, "There will be sent against you both a flame of fire and molten brass" [55:35], and His saying, "They will go around between it and scalding water, intensely hot" [55:44]?

We say: all of these are great bounties, because Allah threatens His servants with them for their reform, so that they leave the realm of disbelief, rebellion, wickedness and disobedience for the realm of obedience, faith, submission and compliance. For whoever warns against the path of destruction, and explains the harm it contains, and urges the path of safety that leads to reward and honour, is a benefactor in the utmost degree and a doer of the utmost good. Similar to this is His saying, "This is what the Most Merciful promised" [36:52]. On this basis, there is suitability for the connection through mention of the attribute of mercy in that context. As for His saying, "Everyone upon it will perish" [55:26], it is a reminder of death and annihilation, to encourage turning towards deeds for the abode of permanence, and turning away from the abode of perishing. The end.

Al-Baghawi said: This verse is repeated in thirty-one places to affirm the bounty and to emphasise the reminder of it. Then He enumerated His blessings to creation, separating each two bounties with what alerts them to it, so that He makes them understand the bounties and confirms them concerning them, like the saying of a man to one who has done him good and bestowed upon him favours while denying and disbelieving them: "Were you not poor and I made you rich? Will you deny this? Were you not naked and I clothed you? Will you deny this? Were you not obscure and I made you honoured? Will you deny this?" Such speech is common in Arabic discourse. The end.

[p-5637] Al-Sayyid Murtada said in al-Durar wal-Ghurar: The repetition in Surat al-Rahman is only made beautiful for the sake of affirming the varied and enumerated bounties. So whenever He mentions a bounty He has bestowed, He rebukes for denial, as a man says to another: "Did I not treat you well by making you wealthy in property? Did I not treat you well by doing such-and-such for you?" So repetition is fitting here, because what is affirmed by it differs, and this is common in Arabic speech and poetry, like the saying of Muhalhil lamenting Kulayb:

"Is it not justice from Kulayb / when the neighbours of the protector are wronged?"

"Is it not justice from Kulayb / when the acacias tremble from the north wind?"

"Is it not justice from Kulayb / when the veiled women come out?"

"Is it not justice from Kulayb / when the secrets of affairs are made public?"

"Is it not justice from Kulayb / when what is feared of the frontiers is feared?"

"Is it not justice from Kulayb / on the day of the great affair's turmoil?"

"Is it not justice from Kulayb / when the protector of the seeker of refuge gives way?"

Then he recited other odes in this pattern, which is one of the subtleties of the Arabs. Understand it.

Shaykh al-Islam said in Mutashabih al-Qur'an: This verse is mentioned thirty-one times. Eight of them are mentioned after verses listing the wonders of Allah's creation and the marvels of His making, and the origin of creation and their return. Then seven of them come after verses mentioning Hell and its severities, corresponding to the number of the gates of Hell. Mentioning the bounties after them is fitting, because among the bounties is the removal of affliction and the postponement of punishment. After these seven, there are eight describing the two gardens and their people, corresponding to the number of the gates of Paradise, and eight more after them, describing the two gardens which are besides the two gardens, taken from His saying, "And besides them are two gardens" [55:62]. Whoever believes in the first eight and acts in accordance with them deserves those two groups of eight from Allah, and is protected from the previous seven. The end.

O Allah, increase us in awareness of the subtleties of Your Noble Qur'an, and in plunging into the pearls of Your Great Criterion.

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ [55:69] ﴿In them are good [women]﴾ [55:70]: this is the plural of khayyirah (good, excellent), with the doubling removed, though it has been read according to the original form, that is, those of excellent character. The choice of the feminine pronoun rather than the dual is out of regard for the word that follows it as its predicate: ﴿beautiful﴾ [55:70], that is, beautiful of face.

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ [55:71] ﴿Maidens, secluded in pavilions﴾ [55:72]. Hur (maidens) is the plural of hawra' (a woman with pure white eyes), meaning the white and pure. The meaning of ﴿secluded﴾ [55:72] is that they have confined themselves to their dwellings, and their only concern is their adornment and their pastimes. The meanings mentioned earlier also apply to it. And ﴿pavilions﴾ [55:72]: Ibn Jarir said: by it is meant houses. The Arabs sometimes call women's litters "pavilions" and he then recited a verse as evidence for this.

﴿In them are women restraining their gaze, whom no man or jinn has touched before them﴾ [55:56]. By these he means the maidens of the two gardens which are besides the first two. Or it is a repetition of what preceded, to draw attention to this attribute, and to its being at the forefront of desirable things and the vanguard of delights:

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ [55:75] ﴿Reclining on cushions﴾ [55:76], that is, couches, or supports, or pillows, ﴿green﴾ [55:76] ﴿and beautiful rugs﴾ [55:76], that is, carpets and mats, ﴿beautiful﴾ [55:76], that is, excellent. The adjective is clarifying, and for this reason Ibn Jubayr said: "The 'abqari' are the finest rugs," that is, their excellent ones.

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ [55:77]: that is, of His honouring the people of His obedience with this honour from you two. ﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honour﴾ [55:78], that is, Possessor of greatness and majesty, of bestowing favours. Here "name" is a metonymy for the Exalted Essence, because the verb mentioned has frequently been joined with it, as in the verse ﴿Blessed is He who placed in the sky constellations﴾ [25:61] and the verse ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is dominion﴾ [67:1], and similar verses. The secret of choosing the word "name" [p-5634] is to draw attention to the fact that from Him, Exalted is He, one knows only His Most Beautiful Names, because it is impossible to comprehend the Holy Essence. ﴿None knows God except God.﴾ This is the verified position.

It has also been said that the word "name" is superfluous, like the verse:

"Until the year's end, then 'peace be upon you both'"

Ibn Hazm held that the "name" remains in its literal sense. He rejected those who argued, from the claim that the name is the named, with an example: there is no proof in what they cited. As for the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, "Blessed is the name of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honour," it is true. The meaning of "tabaraka" is "taf'ala" from "barakah" (blessing). Blessing is due to the name of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, which is a word composed of letters of the alphabet. We seek blessing by mentioning Him, by glorifying Him, by revering and honouring Him. So to Him belongs blessing, and to Him belongs reverence from us and from Allah, Exalted is He, and to Him belongs honour from Allah, Exalted is He, and from us, whether it is written on paper, or on something inscribed in it, or mentioned by tongues. Whoever does not revere the name of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, [p-5635] in this way, nor honours it, is an unbeliever without doubt. So the verse is to be taken in its apparent sense without interpretation, and their clinging to it is thereby void. The end of his words, may Allah have mercy on him.

**Benefit:**

Regarding what the scholars said about the secret of the repetition of "So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?", al-Suyuti said in al-Itqan, in the section on repetition:

Repetition may sometimes not be for emphasis in terms of technical craft, though it is meaningfully emphatic. Among it is that in which a separation occurs between the two repeated items, for emphasis is not separated from what it emphasises.

Then he said: Among this is the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: "So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?" For although it is repeated over thirty-some times, each instance relates to what precedes it, and for this reason it exceeded three. Had all of them referred to one thing, it would not have exceeded three, because emphasis does not exceed that. This was said by Ibn Abd al-Salam and others. The end.

In Arus al-Afrah: If you say: when what is meant by each is what precedes it, is that not elaboration? Rather, they are expressions, each of which is meant to be something other than what the other is meant to be?

I say: If we say that what counts is the generality of the expression, then each one is meant to be what the other is meant to be, but it is repeated so that it is explicit in what follows it and apparent in other respects.

If you say: does that entail emphasis?

I say: The matter is so, and it is not objected that emphasis is not increased beyond three, because that applies to emphasis which is a follower. As for mentioning a thing in more than three separate contexts, there is nothing preventing it. The end.

Al-Izz ibn Abd al-Salam said at the end of his book al-Isharah ila al-Ijaz: As for His saying, "So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?", it may be repeated over all His bounties; it may be that each instance refers to the bounty between it and the one before it; it may be that the first refers to the bounties preceding it, the second to those preceding it, the third to those preceding the first, and the fourth to those preceding the first, second and third, and so on to the end of the surah. [p-5636]

If it is said: how can His saying, "We will attend to you, O two worlds [of men and jinn]" [55:31], be a bounty, and His saying, "The guilty will be known by their marks" [55:41], be a bounty? Likewise, His saying, "This is Hell, which the guilty deny" [55:43], and His saying, "There will be sent against you both a flame of fire and molten brass" [55:35], and His saying, "They will go around between it and scalding water, intensely hot" [55:44]?

We say: all of these are great bounties, because Allah threatens His servants with them for their reform, so that they leave the realm of disbelief, rebellion, wickedness and disobedience for the realm of obedience, faith, submission and compliance. For whoever warns against the path of destruction, and explains the harm it contains, and urges the path of safety that leads to reward and honour, is a benefactor in the utmost degree and a doer of the utmost good. Similar to this is His saying, "This is what the Most Merciful promised" [36:52]. On this basis, there is suitability for the connection through mention of the attribute of mercy in that context. As for His saying, "Everyone upon it will perish" [55:26], it is a reminder of death and annihilation, to encourage turning towards deeds for the abode of permanence, and turning away from the abode of perishing. The end.

Al-Baghawi said: This verse is repeated in thirty-one places to affirm the bounty and to emphasise the reminder of it. Then He enumerated His blessings to creation, separating each two bounties with what alerts them to it, so that He makes them understand the bounties and confirms them concerning them, like the saying of a man to one who has done him good and bestowed upon him favours while denying and disbelieving them: "Were you not poor and I made you rich? Will you deny this? Were you not naked and I clothed you? Will you deny this? Were you not obscure and I made you honoured? Will you deny this?" Such speech is common in Arabic discourse. The end.

[p-5637] Al-Sayyid Murtada said in al-Durar wal-Ghurar: The repetition in Surat al-Rahman is only made beautiful for the sake of affirming the varied and enumerated bounties. So whenever He mentions a bounty He has bestowed, He rebukes for denial, as a man says to another: "Did I not treat you well by making you wealthy in property? Did I not treat you well by doing such-and-such for you?" So repetition is fitting here, because what is affirmed by it differs, and this is common in Arabic speech and poetry, like the saying of Muhalhil lamenting Kulayb:

"Is it not justice from Kulayb / when the neighbours of the protector are wronged?"

"Is it not justice from Kulayb / when the acacias tremble from the north wind?"

"Is it not justice from Kulayb / when the veiled women come out?"

"Is it not justice from Kulayb / when the secrets of affairs are made public?"

"Is it not justice from Kulayb / when what is feared of the frontiers is feared?"

"Is it not justice from Kulayb / on the day of the great affair's turmoil?"

"Is it not justice from Kulayb / when the protector of the seeker of refuge gives way?"

Then he recited other odes in this pattern, which is one of the subtleties of the Arabs. Understand it.

Shaykh al-Islam said in Mutashabih al-Qur'an: This verse is mentioned thirty-one times. Eight of them are mentioned after verses listing the wonders of Allah's creation and the marvels of His making, and the origin of creation and their return. Then seven of them come after verses mentioning Hell and its severities, corresponding to the number of the gates of Hell. Mentioning the bounties after them is fitting, because among the bounties is the removal of affliction and the postponement of punishment. After these seven, there are eight describing the two gardens and their people, corresponding to the number of the gates of Paradise, and eight more after them, describing the two gardens which are besides the two gardens, taken from His saying, "And besides them are two gardens" [55:62]. Whoever believes in the first eight and acts in accordance with them deserves those two groups of eight from Allah, and is protected from the previous seven. The end.

O Allah, increase us in awareness of the subtleties of Your Noble Qur'an, and in plunging into the pearls of Your Great Criterion.
